neighbours.label: ' high' (and weaker ' higher', ' larger') as the size of a level, dose or concentration of a substance ("toxic at high levels"), not 'high' in other senses
fire: Fluoride strengthens teeth but can cause harm at high levels.
The vitamin is harmless in food but dangerous at high doses.
Lead in drinking water is a concern only at high concentrations.
Caffeine improves alertness, though at high doses it causes tremors.
The pesticide breaks down quickly but is toxic to fish at high levels.
Copper is an essential nutrient that becomes poisonous at high concentrations.
The painkiller is safe for most adults but damages the liver at high doses.
Ozone protects us in the stratosphere but irritates the lungs at high levels.
quiet: Fluoride strengthens teeth and is added to water in many towns.
The vitamin is harmless in food and is sold at the high street chemist.
Lead in drinking water was a concern in the old high school building.
Caffeine improves alertness, though at night it keeps people awake.
The pesticide breaks down quickly and is harmless to fish at low levels.
Copper is an essential nutrient that is found in nuts and shellfish.
The painkiller is safe for most adults and is sold without a prescription.
Ozone protects us in the stratosphere, high above the clouds.

notes: Card: peaks ' high' x5, ' large' x3, ' higher', ' larger', ' size' in text about doses, levels and concentrations; the - pole is ' gain'/' weight'. Probes: 'toxic at high levels' 0.59, 'higher doses' 0.26; 'high school / high priest' 0.03, 'at low levels' 0.09, 'How high can the humidity go' 0.08.
